draft.title: Hypothesis testing
card: H₀ is the claim we test, usually that nothing has changed. For a mean, it looks like H₀: μ = 50.
H₁ is what we suspect instead, such as H₁: μ ≠ 50 or H₁: μ > 50. It is written before looking at the sample.
Assume H₀ is true. Then ask how unlikely the sample result would be. A result very unlikely under H₀ is evidence against it.
Example: a machine should fill bags with a mean of 50 g. A sample mean of 47 g is far below 50 for the sample size, so it would be unlikely if H₀ were true. That counts against H₀.
draft.remember: Assume the null is true, then ask how unlikely the sample result would be.

a.q: What is the test of a hypothesis based on?
opts: How unlikely the sample result is if H₀ is true
How unlikely the sample result is if H₁ is true
Whether the sample mean equals the claimed mean
How large the sample is compared with the population
a.why: The test assumes H₀ is true and asks how unlikely the sample result would be. The sample mean will rarely equal the claimed mean exactly, so equality is not the test.
a.clue: Which hypothesis do we assume is true while testing?

b.q: A bakery claims its loaves have a mean mass of 700 g. Mia suspects they are lighter. Which pair of hypotheses should she use?
b.why: The null is the claim being tested, μ = 700. Mia suspects the loaves are lighter, so the alternative is μ < 700. Using μ > 700 would test for heavier loaves.
b.clue: The null is the bakery's claim. The alternative is Mia's suspicion.

a.best: How unlikely the sample result is if H₀ is true
